title: Cap. III Rat. 2: Vasquez — physical vs moral media; no election before works-foresight
latin: Rat. 2. Secundo, argumentatur Vasques a discrimine mediorum Physicorum & Moralium. In Physicis mediis concedit efficacem intentionem finis praecedere intentionem mediorum: at quoties medium ad aliquem finem est morale (qualia sunt opera bona relata ad vitae aeternae consecutionem) negat ullam esse posse efficacem voluntatem in Deo conferendi talem finem ante praescientiam mediorum: Deus ergo non eligit ad gloriam nisi ex praevisione operum, In 1. quaest. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. cap. 9. Vide etiam disp. 81. cap. 5. Esse autem talem differentiam inter media moralia & physica, hinc putat se posse ostendere; quod media physica in se habeant naturalem virtutem causandi finem sine relatione ad voluntatem alterius: ideo licet finis efficaciter intendatur ante praescientiam eorum, ex sua nihilominus virtute, cum adhibentur, conducunt ad finem obtinendum. Jam vero, quia media moralia non producunt finem infra & naturali virtute, sed ex ordinatione alterius, nisi per praescientiam ejus ordinentur & acceptentur ad finem prius quam ille finis efficaciter alicui intentus fuerit, nullius momenti erunt ad finis consecutionem: ut autem acceptentur & ordinentur, praevideri est necesse. Nulla igitur praedestinatio est cujuscunque ad hunc gloriae finem, nisi post praevisionem operum, quae sunt media moralia a Deo ordinata ad eundem.
pass_a: Reason 2. Secondly, Vasquez argues from the discrimination of physical and moral means. In physical means he grants that an efficacious intention of the end precedes the intention of the means: but whenever a means to some end is moral (such as good works related to the obtaining of eternal life) he denies that there can be any efficacious will in God of conferring such an end before the foreknowledge of the means: God therefore does not elect to glory except from the foresight of works, In 1. qu. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. ch. 9. See also disp. 81. ch. 5. And that there is such a difference between moral and physical means, he thinks he can show from this: that physical means have in themselves a natural power of causing the end without relation to another's will: therefore even if the end is efficaciously intended before their foreknowledge, nonetheless by their own power, when they are applied, they conduce to obtaining the end. But now, because moral means do not produce the end by an intrinsic and natural power, but from another's ordination, unless by his foresight they are ordained and accepted to the end before that end has been efficaciously intended for someone, they will be of no moment for obtaining the end: and that they may be accepted and ordained, it is necessary that they be foreseen. Therefore there is no predestination of anyone to this end of glory except after foresight of works, which are moral means ordained by God to the same.
pass_b: Rat. 2. Second, Vasquez argues from the split between physical and moral means. With physical means he grants that an efficacious intention of the end comes before intending the means. But whenever the means to an end is moral (good works ordered to eternal life), he denies God can have any efficacious will to confer that end before foreknowing the means. So God elects to glory only from foresight of works (In 1. q. 23 art. 3 disp. 89 ch. 9; also disp. 81 ch. 5). He thinks he can prove the difference: physical means carry in themselves a natural power to cause the end, without depending on another's will — so even if the end is intended before they are foreknown, when applied they still tend to the end by their own virtue. Moral means, he says, do not produce the end by any inward natural power but only by another's ordination; unless foresight ordains and accepts them to the end before that end is efficaciously intended for someone, they count for nothing toward obtaining it — and to be accepted and ordained they must be foreseen. Hence no one is predestined to glory's end except after foresight of works that are moral means God ordained to that end.

moral means = good works to eternal life

title: Cap. III Resp. Rat. 2: deny the split — end-intention causes means; Paul/grace
latin: Resp. Hoc discrimen inter media physica & moralia, quod Vasques cupit stabilire, nullo modo admittimus. Nam secundum ordinem intentionis (de quo jam quaeritur) finis est causa mediorum tam moralium quam physicorum: atque ex praecedente finis desiderio media haec tum eliguntur tum adhibentur. Nota est regula, Media adhibentur in ordine ad finem. Finis itaque intentio semper praecedit suppeditationem mediorum. Non enim Deus destinasset Paulo efficacem gratiam, nisi prius efficaciter destinasset dare illi gloriam.
pass_a: Response. This discrimination between physical and moral means, which Vasquez desires to establish, we in no way admit. For according to the order of intention (about which the question now is) the end is the cause of means, both moral and physical: and from the preceding desire of the end these means are both chosen and applied. The rule is well known: Means are applied in order to the end. Therefore the intention of the end always precedes the supplying of the means. For God would not have destined efficacious grace to Paul unless he had first efficaciously destined to give him glory.
pass_b: Resp. We do not grant Vasquez's physical/moral split at all. In the order of intention (the real question) the end causes the means — moral as well as physical — and from desiring the end first those means are chosen and applied. Known rule: means are applied toward the end. So intending the end always comes before supplying the means. God would not have destined efficacious grace to Paul unless he had first efficaciously destined to give him glory.

lemmas.lemma: Media adhibentur in ordine ad finem

lemmas.gloss: Paul: grace only after destined glory

title: Cap. III Resp. Rat. 2: execution vs intention — moral/physical mode misses the question
latin: Quod autem attinet ad diversum modum operandi, quem Vasques annotavit in mediis physicis & moralibus, concedimus modo differre; sed negamus hoc causae nostrae obesse. Nam primo, illa sua consideratione aberrat a scopo controversiae. Quaeritur enim non de ordine exsecutionis, in quo fatemur media relata ad finem habere rationem causae ad effectum; sed de ordine intentionis, in quo media comparantur ad finem tanquam effecta ad causam. Quae autem ille philosophatur de diversitate operandi inter media physica & moralia, spectant ad finem, non qua consideratur in voluntate & mente agentis, sed qua consideratur ut posita in exsecutione externa: quo sensu, perspicuum est media praecedere finem: Sed ad rem non facit.
pass_a: But as for the diverse mode of operating which Vasquez noted in physical and moral means, we grant that they differ in mode; yet we deny that this hurts our cause. For first, that consideration of his wanders from the scope of the controversy. For the question is not about the order of execution, in which we confess that means related to the end have the character of a cause toward the effect; but about the order of intention, in which means are compared to the end as effects to a cause. But what he philosophizes about the diversity of operating between physical and moral means looks to the end not as considered in the will and mind of the agent, but as considered as placed in external execution: in which sense it is clear that means precede the end: But it does not touch the point.
pass_b: As for Vasquez's different operating mode in physical vs moral means: we grant they differ in mode, but deny that hurts our case. First, that angle misses the controversy's aim. We are not asking about execution-order — where we admit means related to the end act as cause toward the effect — but about intention-order, where means stand to the end as effects to a cause. His philosophy about how physical and moral means operate looks to the end as already out in external execution, not as in the agent's will and mind. In that sense means do precede the end — but that is beside the point.

lemmas.gloss: in intention, means are effects of the end

title: Cap. III Resp. Rat. 2: moral means foreknown as apt/possible — not absolutely future before election
latin: Secundo, quod urget nullius momenti fore media moralia ad ipsam consecutionem finis, nisi fuissent praevisa & acceptata a Deo ante efficacem intentionem finis, fatemur talia media habere suam vim causandi finem, sive operandi ad consecutionem finis, a praecedente voluntate Dei, qui ea ordinavit & acceptavit ad talem finem: sed simul affirmamus, haec media praecognosci & praevideri a Deo antequam finis intendatur, solummodo tanquam apta & conducentia ad finem, tanquam possibilia & communicabilia illis omnibus quibus vult finem; sed non praesciuntur & praevidentur tanquam absolute futura in hoc aut illo singulari homine, priusquam sit efficaciter ad gloriam electus, id est, ad finem destinatus.
pass_a: Secondly, as to what he urges — that moral means will be of no moment for the very obtaining of the end unless they had been foreseen and accepted by God before the efficacious intention of the end — we confess that such means have their force of causing the end, or of operating toward obtaining the end, from the preceding will of God who ordained and accepted them to such an end: but at the same time we affirm that these means are foreknown and foreseen by God before the end is intended only as apt and conducive to the end, as possible and communicable to all those for whom he wills the end; but they are not foreknown and foreseen as absolutely future in this or that singular man before he is efficaciously elected to glory, that is, destined to the end.
pass_b: Second, he presses that moral means would be worthless for obtaining the end unless foreseen and accepted by God before an efficacious intention of the end. We grant such means get their power to cause — or work toward — the end from God's prior will that ordained and accepted them to that end. But we also affirm: before the end is intended, God foreknows those means only as apt and helpful to it, as possible and shareable with all for whom he wills the end — not as absolutely going to happen in this or that particular person before that person is efficaciously elected to glory (destined to the end).

title: Cap. III Resp. Rat. 2 close: Semipelagian charge — Augustine election yields faith/sanctity/perseverance
latin: Postremo, in hoc suo argumento Vasques transit in castra Semipelagianorum, & Augustinum deserit, qui passim docet, non eligi homines ad vitam aeternam ex praescientia fidei aut bonorum operum, sed inde potius oriri omnia nostra bona opera, quod fuimus praedestinati ad vitam aeternam. Hinc fides: Non eliguntur quia crediderunt, sed eliguntur ut credant, De Praedest. sanct. lib. 1. cap. 17. Hinc sanctitas: Certum & manifestum est, ideo nos sanctos futuros, quia elegit nos Deus, praedestinans ut per gratiam tales essemus: ibid. cap. 18. Hinc perseverantia: Sanctis in regnum Dei per gratiam praedestinatis, donatur ipsa perseverantia, De corr. & gratia, cap. 12. Post electionem igitur omnia nostra bona praevidentur, quia ab electione ipsa proficiscuntur.
pass_a: Finally, in this argument of his Vasquez crosses into the camp of the Semipelagians, and deserts Augustine, who everywhere teaches that men are not elected to eternal life from foresight of faith or of good works, but that rather all our good works arise from this, that we were predestined to eternal life. Hence faith: They are not elected because they believed, but they are elected that they may believe, De praedestinatione sanctorum book 1 chapter 17. Hence holiness: It is certain and manifest that therefore we are to be holy, because God elected us, predestining that through grace we should be such: ibid. chapter 18. Hence perseverance: To the saints predestined by grace into the kingdom of God, perseverance itself is given, De correptione et gratia chapter 12. After election, therefore, all our goods are foreseen, because they proceed from election itself.
pass_b: Finally, in this argument Vasquez crosses into the Semipelagian camp and leaves Augustine, who everywhere teaches men are not elected to eternal life from foresight of faith or good works — rather all our good works arise because we were predestined to eternal life. Faith: not elected because they believed, but elected that they may believe (De praed. sanct. 1.17). Holiness: certain and plain we will be holy because God elected us, predestining that by grace we should be such (ibid. 18). Perseverance: to saints predestined by grace into God's kingdom, perseverance itself is given (De corr. et grat. 12). So after election all our goods are foreseen, because they spring from election itself.
